source_text: (Sed Christus diuortium inhibet dicens: qui dimiserit uxorem suam et aliam duxerit, adulterium committet, (et) qui dimissam a uiro duxerit, aeque adulter est, - ut sic quoque prohibeat diuortium, inlicitum facit repudiatae matrimonium — Moyses uero permittit repudium in Deuteronomio: si sumserit quis uxorem et habitauerit cum ea, et euenerit non inuenire eam apud eum gratiam, eo quod inuentum sit in illa impudicum negotium, scribet libellum repudii et dabit in manu eius et dimittet illam de domo sua. uides diuersitatem legis et euangelii, Moysi et Christi\'? plane. non enim recepisti illud quoque euangelium eiusdem ueritatis et eiusdem Christi, in quo prohibens diuortium propriam quaestionem eius absoluit: Moyses propter duritiam cordis uestri praecepit libellum repudii dare; a primordio autem non fuit sic; quia scilicet qui marem et feminam fecerat, erunt duo, dixerat, in carne una; quod deus itaque iunxit, homo (non) disiunxerit. hoc enim responso et Moysi constitutionem protexit, ut sui, et creatoris institutionem direxit, ut Christus ipsius. sed quatenus ex his reuincendus es, quae recepisti, sic tibi occurram, ac si meus Christus (tuus:) nonne et ipse prohibens diuortium et parem tamen gestans eius, qui marem et feminam iunxit, excusauerit potius quam destruxerit Moysi constitutionem? sed ecce sic tuus sit iste Christus contrarium docens Moysi et creatori, ut, si non contrarium ostendero, meus sit. dico enim illum condicionaliter nunc fecisse diuortii prohibitionem, si ideo quis dimittat uxoiem, ut aliam ducat: qui dimiserit, inquit, uxorem et aliam duxerit, adulterium commisit, et qui a marito dimissam duxerit aeque adulter est, ex eadem utique causa dimissam, qua non licet dimitti, ut alia ducatur; inlicite enim dimissam pro indimissa ducens adulter est. manet enim matrimonium quod non rite diremptum est; manente (autem) matrimonio nubere adulterium est. ita si condicionaliter prohibuit dimittere uxorem, non in totum prohibuit, et quod non prohibuit in totum, permisit alias, ubi causa cessat, ob quam prohibuit; et iam non contrarium Moysi docet, cuius praeceptum alicubi conseruat, nondum dico confirmat. aut si omnino [non] negas permitti diuortium a \' Christo, quomodo tu nuptias dirimis, nec coniungens marem et feminam nec alibi coniunctos ad sacramentum baptismatis et eucharistiae admittens, nisi inter se coniurauerint aduersus fructum nuptiarum, ut aduersus ipsum creatorem? certe quid faciet apud te maritus, si uxor eius commiserit adulterium? habebitne illam? sed nec tuum apostolum sinere (scis) coniungi prostitutae membra Christi. habet itaque et Christum adsertorem iustitia diuortii. iam hinc confirmatur ab illo Moyses ex eodem titulo perhibens repudium, quo et Christus: si inuentum fuerit in muliere negotium impudicum. nam et in euangelio Mathei: qui dimiserit, inquit, uxorem suam praeter causam adulterii, facit eam adulterari. atque ita adulter censetur et ille, qui dimissam a uiro duxerit.
pass_a_gloss: But Christ inhibits divorce, saying: he who dismisses his wife and marries another, commits adultery, and he who marries a woman dismissed by her husband is just as much an adulterer, - so that in this way also he prohibits divorce, he makes the marriage of the repudiated woman illicit — Moses, however, permits repudiation in Deuteronomy: if someone takes a wife and lives with her, and it happens that he does not find her pleasing to him, because some indecent matter is found in her, he will write a certificate of repudiation and give it into her hand and dismiss her from his house. You see the difference between the law and the gospel, between Moses and Christ? Clearly. For you have not received that gospel of the same truth and of the same Christ, in which, while prohibiting divorce, he resolves his own question: Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, commanded to give a certificate of repudiation; but from the beginning it was not so; because, clearly, the one who made male and female said that the two will be one flesh; what God, therefore, has joined, let man not separate. For with this response, he both protected Moses' constitution, as his own, and directed the institution of the Creator, as Christ himself. But insofar as you are to be convicted from these things, which you have received, I will meet you as if my Christ were yours: does he not, while prohibiting divorce and yet bearing the same attitude as the one who joined male and female, rather excuse than destroy Moses' constitution? But, behold, if your Christ is such, teaching the opposite of Moses and the Creator, so that, if I do not show the opposite, he is mine. For I say that he conditionally made the prohibition of divorce now, if someone dismisses his wife in order to marry another: he who dismisses his wife and marries another, commits adultery, and he who marries a woman dismissed by her husband is just as much an adulterer, from the same cause for which she was dismissed, for which it is not lawful to dismiss her, in order to marry another; for he who marries a woman illicitly dismissed, as if she were not dismissed, is an adulterer. For the marriage remains which has not been lawfully dissolved; and with the marriage remaining, to marry is adultery. Thus, if he conditionally prohibited dismissing a wife, he did not prohibit it entirely, and what he did not entirely prohibit, he permitted in other cases, where the cause for which he prohibited it ceases; and now he does not teach the opposite of Moses, whose precept he preserves somewhere, not to mention confirms. Or, if you entirely deny that Christ permits divorce, how do you dissolve marriages, neither joining male and female nor admitting those already joined to the sacrament of baptism and the Eucharist, unless they have sworn against the fruit of marriage, so against the Creator himself? Certainly, what will a husband do with you, if his wife commits adultery? Will he keep her? But neither does your apostle allow the members of Christ to be joined to a prostitute. Therefore, Christ also asserts the justice of divorce. Now from this it is confirmed by him that Moses, from the same title, permits repudiation, as also Christ: if an indecent matter is found in a woman. For also in the gospel of Matthew: he who dismisses his wife, he says, except for the cause of adultery, makes her an adulteress. And thus the one who marries a woman dismissed by her husband is also considered an adulterer.

bible_refs.note: Christ's teaching on divorce in Matthew

pass_b_english: Christ forbids divorce, saying that whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband is equally an adulterer — so that in this way too he blocks divorce by making the marriage of the repudiated woman illicit. Moses, however, permits repudiation in Deuteronomy: if a man takes a wife and lives with her, and it happens that he finds no favor in her because some indecent matter is found in her, he shall write a certificate of divorce, give it into her hand, and send her from his house (Deuteronomy). You see the difference between the law and the gospel, between Moses and Christ? Obviously. For you have not accepted that gospel of the same truth and the same Christ, in which, while prohibiting divorce, he answers his own question: Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, commanded you to give a certificate of divorce; but from the beginning it was not so, for the one who made male and female said the two shall become one flesh; what God has joined together, let no one separate (Matthew). By that answer he both safeguarded Moses' statute as his own and upheld the Creator's institution as Christ himself. But to the extent you must be convicted from the texts you have accepted, I will meet you on your own ground, as if my Christ were yours: does he not, while forbidding divorce yet sharing the mind of the one who joined male and female, rather vindicate than demolish Moses' statute? But look — if your Christ teaches the opposite of Moses and the Creator, then he is mine if I do not prove the contrary. For I say he imposed the divorce prohibition conditionally: if a man dismisses his wife in order to marry another, he who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman dismissed by her husband is equally an adulterer, on the very ground for which she was dismissed — a ground on which dismissal is not lawful — so that another may be taken; for he who marries a woman illicitly dismissed, as though she were not dismissed, is an adulterer. The marriage remains, since it has not been lawfully dissolved; and while the marriage endures, to marry again is adultery. Thus, if he prohibited dismissing a wife only conditionally, he did not prohibit it entirely, and what he did not wholly prohibit he permitted in other cases where the cause for the prohibition ceases; and so he no longer teaches the opposite of Moses, whose precept he preserves somewhere, not to say confirms. Or if you deny outright that Christ permits divorce, how do you dissolve marriages, neither joining male and female nor admitting those already joined to the sacrament of baptism and the Eucharist, unless they have sworn against the fruit of marriage — that is, against the Creator himself? What will a husband do with you if his wife commits adultery? Keep her? But your own apostle does not allow the members of Christ to be joined to a prostitute. Therefore Christ too upholds the justice of divorce. Now this is confirmed by Moses on the same ground on which Christ also permits repudiation: if an indecent matter is found in a woman. For in Matthew's gospel: whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of adultery, makes her an adulteress; and thus the man who marries a woman dismissed by her husband is also counted an adulterer (Matthew).
notes: The translation aims to follow the Latin text closely, while providing a clear and accurate English rendering.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex conditional arguments regarding the legality of divorce and the relationship between Mosaic law and Christ's teaching. All scripture citations (Deuteronomy, Matthew) are correctly identified and applied to the relevant clauses. Pass A preserves the nuances of the Latin (e.g., 'condicionaliter', 'inlicite dimissam') and Pass B maintains fidelity without adding external meaning.
